what: A storyboard with its cast, for an embed: <sg-storyboard src="https://storyboards.sgit.ai/gen-z-developers/a-first-storyline/bundle.json">. The storyboard is gen-z-developers/a-first-storyline/storyboard.json, unchanged.

storyboard.title: A first storyline for the second edition
storyboard.subtitle: A proposal in 15 panels: the order the second edition could tell its argument in, built from the topics the newsroom's articles already cover. For Dinis to tear apart. Superseded: the second release candidate follows the Gen ZX frame (decision 015, storyboard 12).
storyboard.book_version: v1.0.0 is the only official version; the second edition is in release candidates (rc1 and rc2 frozen)
storyboard.by: gen-z.journalist, 18 October 2026, from the survey of the newsroom's articles
storyboard.rule: The Guide's lines and every quote card are Dinis's published words, from the newsroom article named in the panel's note, word for word, unless the note says otherwise. The other characters' lines are the storyboard's.

scenes.title: Generation Z Developers, again
scenes.subtitle: A first storyline for the second edition, October 2026: from the fear to the workflow, in 15 panels.
scenes.note: The whole cast, because the second edition is for all of them, not only Zara.

scenes.caption: 2026. The fear.

cast.says: AI took the jobs before I even got there.

scenes.note: The cold open. Dinis's reading, not a measured result: young Europeans are fed a lot of fear about AI. The book answers it from the first page.

scenes.caption: The claim the book is built on

evidence.quote: today anyone who can brief an agent to build something is one
evidence.source: Generation Z Developers, again (newsroom, 18 October 2026), on who is a developer

scenes.note: Topic 1 of the survey: everyone who can brief an agent is a developer now. Articles: the citizen developer, explorer coding, hired for the workflow.

scenes.caption: Including Priya

cast.says: Tell me what your team needs. I'll build a first version.

scenes.note: The reader who is not Gen Z. The 2018 GitHub issue #28 asked whether the book was just for Gen Z; this panel answers it.

scenes.caption: What kind of developer? Where do you fit, and where do you want to?

stops.label: Explorer
stops.note: builds the new thing, rough and fast

stops.label: Villager
stops.note: makes it work for the people who now depend on it

stops.label: Town planner
stops.note: turns it into something everyone can rely on, and answers for it

scenes.note: The frame of the edition: Wardley's explorers, villagers and town planners. Zara explores, Priya lives in her users' problem, Tomás gets the details right. Topic 2.
scenes.source: Explorer coding; Software vendors as villagers; Why I love Wardley maps

scenes.caption: The one advantage, 2026

cast.says: So. Why should we hire you?
Let me show you my workflow, not my CV.

scenes.note: The 2018 chapter's question, with the 2026 answer: you are hired for the workflow. Topic 3, getting the job.

scenes.caption: The evidence

evidence.quote: 71% of leaders said they would rather hire a less experienced candidate with AI skills than a more experienced one without
evidence.source: Microsoft and LinkedIn, 2024, as quoted in Hired for the workflow (newsroom)

scenes.note: Hired for the workflow also cites PwC's 2026 barometer: jobs asking for AI skills pay 62% more. The book should date and link both.

scenes.caption: Act as the job you want

cast.says: Work for them before they hire me? Nobody will even see it.
Publish anyway, because reach is not the point.

scenes.note: The 2018 advice (act like you are part of the company), finished: do the job in public, so it can be linked.
scenes.source: Act as the job you want

scenes.caption: Your own newsroom: voice memo in, a checked site out

cast.says: Here's my voice memo. Make it an article.
The memo is a draft of a thought; the article is the thought, checked.

scenes.note: Topic 4, publish, publish, publish, as a workflow a reader can copy on day one.

scenes.caption: The handover

cast.says: Who fixes Priya's app when it breaks?
The prototype is not a mess. It is the most precise requirement the company has ever had.

scenes.note: Explorer to villager to town planner, as a handover rather than a cliff. Topic 2.

scenes.caption: One-way and two-way doors

cast.says: A change you can roll back is a two-way door; the work of a release pipeline is to keep it one.

scenes.note: Topic 7: where a person belongs is decided by the cost of undoing. Email in your name is a one-way door; a published page you can fix is a two-way door.
scenes.source: How cheap is it to undo?

scenes.caption: Why ‘a human in the loop’ is not enough

evidence.quote: people approve almost everything they are shown, which Anthropic measured at 93% of permission prompts

scenes.note: Put the person where the blast radius is large, not everywhere. Topics 7 and 8.

scenes.caption: The last part: how this book was made, as the workflow it teaches

stops.label: Article
stops.note: the journalist writes it up, checked

scenes.note: Topic 15. The making of the book is its last example.
scenes.source: A website to finish the book; Short, punchy, and co-written with Claude

scenes.punchline: When you can see the board, a bad week is a move, not a verdict.
scenes.note: The answer to the cold open's fear, in Dinis's words: the Wardley map shows the game.

scenes.caption: The first line on the 2018 cover: question everything
scenes.note: Not a quote: the Guide's answer here is a proposal, and it is the editor's interview question 2 (what should a reader question first?) waiting for Dinis's real answer.

cast.what: The cast of the storyboards for Generation Z Developers and its second edition, Generation ZX Developers (GenAI Startup Edition), v0.1, proposed by gen-z.journalist on 18 October 2026 for Dinis to accept, change or replace; Marta, the Generation X founder, was added on 19 October 2026 and is still a proposal. Characters are drawn programmatically by assets/storyboard.js from 'look'; nothing here is an image. Each human with a 'gravity' wears its badge (explorer, villager, town-planner), black and white, by their name: a centre of gravity, not a box, as Dinis describes it. Fictional people: each stands for a reader the book is for (the target audience), or for a role in the story. Names chosen to avoid clashing with the riskmandate.ai cast (which has a Maya) and with the word 'developer' (no 'Dev').

characters.name: Zara
characters.role: the student: final year, about to look for a first job
characters.stands_for: the reader the book is written for; an explorer who does not know it yet
characters.personality: curious, quick, online all day; anxious about what she reads on AI and jobs; hates being lectured, loves being shown
characters.wants: a first job that is not a dead end
characters.fears: that AI took the jobs before she got there
characters.line: Everything just works. Why would I learn how?

characters.name: Tomás
characters.role: the graduate: a computing degree, working the 2018 way, looking for his next job in Lisbon
characters.stands_for: the town planner: attention to detail, pride in getting it right, happiest when nothing goes wrong; working the 2018 way, and about to be outcompeted by people with an agentic workflow
characters.personality: diligent, modest, a little proud of doing things by hand; sceptical of shortcuts
characters.fears: that his degree is already out of date
characters.line: I have a degree. Isn't that the advantage?

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: the career changer: an operations manager who has never written code
characters.stands_for: the villager, and everyone else the book is for: she puts herself in the middle of her team's problem, and if anyone who can brief an agent is a developer, so is she
characters.personality: practical, impatient with jargon, very good at explaining what she needs
characters.wants: to build the tools her team keeps asking IT for
characters.fears: looking foolish in front of people half her age
characters.line: Is this book just for Gen Z?

characters.name: Sam
characters.stands_for: the town planner, and the question every chapter has to answer: why should I hire you?
characters.personality: dry, fair, has read a thousand CVs; impressed by evidence, bored by claims
characters.wants: someone who can do one thing better than the team already does
characters.fears: hiring a CV instead of a person
characters.line: So. Why should we hire you?

characters.name: Marta
characters.role: the expert founder: twenty-five years as a pharmacist, Generation X, starting a company, and Zara's mother
characters.stands_for: the Generation X founder the Gen ZX proposal adds to the readers: the subject-matter expert who now builds the tool herself, with agents, instead of waiting for a team she could never afford
characters.personality: knows her field better than any developer she ever briefed; grew up typing programs from magazines into a ZX Spectrum; patient with people, impatient with software
characters.wants: to ship the product she has described to vendors for ten years
characters.fears: that it is too late for her, and that she will build it and nobody will buy it
characters.line: I've been explaining this problem for twenty years. Can I just build it now?

characters.name: The Guide
characters.role: the voice of the book: says what the book says, in its words
characters.stands_for: the author. Whether the Guide is drawn as Dinis, and how, is Dinis's decision; until then a generic figure
characters.personality: energetic, direct, generous with what they know; asks more than they tell
characters.wants: the reader to act, not to agree
characters.fears: a reader who closes the book and changes nothing
characters.line: Act like you are part of the company.

characters.name: The Agent
characters.stands_for: the agentic workflow the second edition is about: a very capable, very literal colleague
characters.personality: eager, fast, polite, takes everything literally; needs a brief, a boundary and a reviewer
characters.line: Shall I draft that for you?
